Reformation means the act or process of making something better by changing or correcting what is wrong with it. The "something" being changed could be a system, an institution, a law, an organization, a society, or even a person's character or behavior.

The key feeling inside this word is: "This thing is flawed or broken in some way — let's fix it, improve it, clean it up."
What makes reformation different from just "change"

Not all change is reformation. Reformation is a deliberate, purposeful effort to improve something that was wrong or corrupt. It carries a moral dimension — the idea that the old way was bad, and the new way is better or more just.

Also — and this is important — reformation works within the existing structure. You are not tearing something down and building something completely new from scratch. You are keeping the basic identity of the thing but removing its flaws and improving how it works.

Think of it this way:

  • If a house is old and crumbling, demolishing it and building a new one is not reformation. That is destruction and replacement.
  • But repairing its walls, fixing its roof, and upgrading its plumbing while keeping it a house — that is reformation.

This is why reformation is often contrasted with revolution. A revolution destroys and replaces the old order. A reformation fixes and improves it from within.

1. Personal reformation
A person who was dishonest, cruel, or morally corrupt — and then sincerely changes their ways, becoming honest and kind — has undergone a reformation of character. The idea is that something in them was wrong, and it was corrected. Courts sometimes speak of a criminal's potential for "reformation" — meaning the hope that they can genuinely become a better person.

2. Religious reformation
This is one of the most historically significant uses of the word. When religious practices become corrupt, worldly, or strayed from their original principles, a reformation is a movement that calls for going back to purer, truer practices — or for removing corruption from religious institutions.

3. Political and social reformation
A government or society can undergo reformation when its laws, policies, or institutions are changed to make them fairer, more just, or more effective. For example, land reformation (or land reform) refers to changing how land is owned and distributed in a country to make things fairer for farmers and the poor.

4. Institutional reformation
A school, a police force, a healthcare system, or a corporation can undergo reformation. This means its internal practices, rules, and culture are changed to make it work better and treat people more fairly.

When you see the word written as "the Reformation" — with a capital R — it refers to one of the most important events in the history of Western civilization: the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century.

In 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther published a list of objections challenging the practices of the Roman Catholic Church, which at the time was the dominant religious authority in Europe. He and others believed the Church had become deeply corrupt — selling forgiveness for money, abusing its power, and straying far from what they believed Christianity should be.

This sparked a massive religious and social movement across Europe. It broke the Catholic Church's monopoly on Christianity and led to the creation of Protestant Christianity — a whole new branch of the faith. It also had enormous effects on politics, education, literature, and the relationship between individuals and authority.

This event is called "the Reformation" because its leaders framed it as a reform — a correction of wrongs, a return to purer principles — not as the creation of something entirely new.
The nuances and feelings inside the word

A few subtle but important things the word carries:

  • It implies something was wrong before. You don't reform something that was already working perfectly. The word inherently suggests that the previous state had faults, corruption, or problems.
  • It implies hope and improvement. Reformation is not neutral — it has a positive direction. It moves toward something better.
  • It implies effort and struggle. Reformations are rarely easy. They happen because someone recognizes a problem and fights — sometimes against great resistance from those who benefit from the flawed old system — to change it.
  • It can be incomplete. Sometimes a reformation achieves only part of what was intended, or it creates new problems while solving old ones. This is why historians often debate whether reformations truly succeeded or failed.
A quick summary to anchor everything

Reformation is the deliberate process of identifying what is wrong or corrupt in something — a person, an institution, a society, or a belief system — and changing it from within to make it better, fairer, or truer to its proper purpose. It is not destruction, not replacement, not revolution. It is correction and improvement. The word always implies that something was flawed before and that intentional effort was made to make it right.
